newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian region starts voting in symbolic election.
newsitem.headline: Russian region starts voting in symbolic election.

text.p: Russia's dynamic Nizhny Novgorod region voted for a new governor on Sunday in a run-off poll between a Communist and reformist that could have a ripple effect on the future of reforms in the entire country.
On the face of it, the vote is simply to replace Boris Nemtsov, summoned by President Boris Yeltsin in March to join his team as a first deputy prime minister and speed up reforms.

But the election -- a closely fought race between the reformist mayor of Nizhny Novgorod city, Ivan Sklyarov, and Communist Gennady Khodyrev -- is an unofficial referendum on the country's painful transition to a market economy.
The men finished almost neck and neck in the first round two weeks ago. Voting started at 6 a.m. (0200 GMT) on Sunday and ends at 11 p.m. (1900 GMT). Results are not expected before Monday.
Voting began relatively slowly in cool and cloudy weather. Mainly elderly people were seen at polling stations.

"I hope later in the day younger people will start turning out more actively because the more young people come to vote the better Sklyarov's chances are," Ivan Pereverzev, an observer for the Sklyarov campaign team, told Reuters.

"This election will show whether the people of Nizhny Novgorod region appreciate the changes over the past six years and want reforms to continue," the newspaper Birzha said, adding the vote was crucicial for Nemtsov and reforms.

Nemtsov, a liberal who pioneered economic change in his region after he became governor in 1991, is now a key member of Yeltsin's reshuffled cabinet and is committed to a series of radical economic steps intended to revitalise reforms.

"If people reject reforms in his domain, how can he offer them for the rest of Russia?" Birzha said. Nemtsov is widely seen as the standard bearer of radical reform and a potential successor to Yeltsin.
Nemtsov transformed Nizhny Novgorod, a city of 1.5 million people on the Volga some 420 km (260 miles) southeast of Moscow.
Clean and businesslike, the city's streets are full of new shops and crowded cafes -- a striking contrast to many other depressed and declining regional centres.
Local Communist leaders noted after the first round that even among regional industrial workers, their traditional electorate, many had supported Nemtsov's reforms.
"Many workers are blinded by capitalist propaganda," the Communist Vybor Naroda (People's Choice) newspaper complained.

But the outcome of Sunday's vote is far from clear. The Communists still have a vast field of disciplined potential voters, many awaiting pay packets due months ago. Support is also strong in rural areas.

The Communists can hope for the votes of many impoverished pensioners, who make up a third of the region's four-million-strong population, although Moscow recently fulfilled its promise to pay pension arrears.
One elderly woman who gave her name as Baba (Granny) Masha said: "I wanted to vote for Khodyrev first but Sklyarov payed my pension a month ago so I decided to vote for him."

Communist officials from Moscow rushed to Nizhny Novgorod to back Khodyrev, 55, who ruled the region as a party chief in the late 1980s and later became a sugar trader. He is also backed, surprisingly, by nationalist maverick Vladimir Zhirinovsky.
Nemtsov visited the region last week to campaign for Sklyarov, who is 49 and less charismatic than his predecessor.
